title: Calais — the train this whole route exists for
learning_goal: Know that our train is the Indian Mail, that it could only run because rails reached Brindisi in 1865 and the canal opened in 1869, and that the first P&O sailing from Brindisi was two years before Fogg; feel the border arrive as a sound.

narration.script:
The boat comes in beside the railway station quay — le quai — and hands you to the train. Customs officers in green and grey. Touts shouting English the way the French hear it. Hot coffee at one in the morning.

This is the train. In French, la malle des Indes — the India mail. It runs from Calais to Brindisi to meet a ship. It exists because of three dates: rails reached the heel in 1865, the Suez Canal opened in 1869, and the first steamer left Brindisi for India in October 1870. Two years before Fogg.

In the novel, when the bank is robbed, detectives go to six ports. Brindisi is one, and nobody needs it explained.

One last thing about the night train to Paris. It runs through Amiens — where Jules Verne had been living for a year, writing this book.

production_notes: SEGMENT 3, second half (80 s; the segment's ceiling is 215 words and this scene spends 147 of the 68 the quiz did not). NO LISTS ALOUD (style guide, persona §2.6): Verne's six ports are counted, not recited — 'detectives are sent to six ports. Brindisi is one of them.' The three dates ARE spoken because three is the limit of a breath and they are the argument of the segment. F-108 IS NOT NARRATED anywhere: the postcard's printed claim is a caption (a quotation of the artefact) plus one go-deeper pin phrased as an open question, exactly as instructed; the guide never says the train carried no passengers. AMIENS: 'where Jules Verne had been living for a year, writing this book' — never 'the house he wrote it in' (F-80's own note: the museum house is the one he took in 1882). GLOSS CHIPS: only two, and both gloss words the guide actually speaks — 'le quai' at ~6 s and 'la malle des Indes' at ~26 s. The rundown also asked for 'la douane' and 'le buffet'; both are CUT, because the guide says 'customs officers' and 'hot coffee' in English and a chip may never gloss a word the traveller does not hear.
